evidence_notes.research_design: PairCoder assigns reflection, diverse plan generation and selection, loop detection, and repair direction to a Navigator while a Driver implements, executes, and repairs code. Both roles use the same foundation model within a run. The evaluation uses GPT-3.5-turbo-0613 and DeepSeek-Coder-Instruct-33B on HumanEval, HumanEval+, MBPP, MBPP+, and CodeContest validation/test, with an additional GPT-4 comparison. The Navigator samples 15 plans at temperature 0.8, clusters them into three representatives with text-embedding-3-large and k-means++, and otherwise uses greedy decoding. Public tests drive at most 10 generation/repair iterations; hidden tests determine greedy pass@1. Component ablations remove multi-plan exploration or feedback-driven refinement, and a cost study logs GPT-3.5 API calls and input-plus-output tokens.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: For reproduced conditions, the foundation model, 16K context limit, problem descriptions, public tests, Python 3.9 execution environment, and maximum of 10 code generation/refinement attempts are held constant. A later comparison also permits direct, CoT, SCoT, Self-planning, and Self-repair up to 10 attempts. The comparison is not fully budget matched: PairCoder additionally samples and embeds plans, uses separate role prompts and historical memory, and consumes different actual calls and tokens. Some GPT-4 and multi-agent baseline values are borrowed from prior papers. No monolithic single-agent controller receives the same candidate plans, execution transcript, memory, and total inference budget.
headline_results: With GPT-3.5, PairCoder reaches 87.80% pass@1 on HumanEval and 15.15% on CodeContest-test, versus 67.68% and 6.06% for direct prompting. With DeepSeek-Coder it reaches 85.37% and 14.55%, versus 76.22% and 6.67%. The reported relative gains are largest on CodeContest, where initial plans fail more often.

Under the later common ceiling of 10 attempts, PairCoder still reaches 87.80%, 80.60%, and 15.15% on HumanEval, MBPP, and CodeContest-test, versus direct prompting at 75.61%, 72.80%, and 9.09%; equal attempt ceilings therefore do not erase the system-level advantage, although actual calls and tokens remain unequal.

Ablation supports both mechanisms. On GPT-3.5 CodeContest-test, full PairCoder scores 15.15%, versus 10.91% without multi-plan exploration and 9.69% without feedback-driven refinement. The paper reports larger relative component effects on CodeContest-test than HumanEval.

The gain costs more inference. On HumanEval, PairCoder averages 5.28 calls and 5.98 thousand tokens per problem versus 2.43 calls and 1.19 thousand tokens for repeated direct prompting. On CodeContest-test, the corresponding figures are 17.56 calls and 24.06 thousand tokens versus 8.73 and 9.79 thousand.

Reliability remains bounded by visible tests. PairCoder passes public versus private tests on 95.73% versus 87.80% of HumanEval tasks and 21.21% versus 15.15% of CodeContest-test tasks; CodeContest-test failures include 60.00% wrong answers, 16.36% runtime errors, and 8.48% time-limit errors.

The evidence covers isolated Python functions and competition problems, not repository-scale development, deployed services, maintainability, or production incidents. No security or generated-code sandbox evaluation is reported.
limitations: Role count is not isolated from plan sampling, embedding-based clustering, memory, execution feedback, and additional inference, so the study establishes a PairCoder system advantage rather than a pure two-agent causal effect.
Public-test availability and coverage directly constrain repair; passing sparse visible tests does not guarantee hidden-test correctness.
The evaluation is limited to Python benchmark and competition tasks, two main model families, zero-shot prompts, and no repository-level or production workflow.
Plan sampling is stochastic, but repeated-run variance, confidence intervals, and significance tests for architecture differences are not reported.
Benchmark contamination may inflate absolute results, and the paper does not measure monetary cost, latency, energy, security defects, or safe execution of generated code.
future_work: Validate PairCoder across broader LLM families, benchmarks, and multilingual code generation.
Explore effective few-shot prompting rather than the evaluated zero-shot setting.
Integrate human feedback or external knowledge to improve Navigator planning.
Combine retrieval augmentation and test-case generation with the existing repair loop.
combinable_methods: Diverse plan sampling and representative-plan clustering followed by execution-guided selection.
Historical code-and-feedback memory that switches plans when a repair state repeats.
Feedback-driven repair using trusted public tests, augmented with generated edge cases or broader test suites.
Runtime block-level debugging such as LDB inside the Navigator-Driver repair stages.
Human or retrieved external knowledge for high-level planning, with bounded iterations and call/token accounting.

evidence_notes.research_design: A tester agent first produces a binary vulnerability judgment and short rationale, then a developer agent receives it and the two exchange queries, deductions, and insights until consensus or a maximum depth of five rounds; the tester's latest judgment is final. Every agent and the single-role baseline use gpt-3.5-turbo-0125. Basic and chain-of-thought prompts are evaluated on C/C++ code segments for function-call, arithmetic-expression, array-usage, and pointer-usage vulnerabilities. Three 1,000-item groups vary vulnerable prevalence from 80% to 50% to 20%, and precision, recall, and F1 are reported.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: The single-role and multi-role conditions use the same GPT-3.5 model version, code dataset, vulnerability categories, and basic or CoT prompt family. The architecture comparison is not inference-budget matched: multi-role discussion allows up to five rounds of 120 tokens and consumes 484% more tokens. The paper does not provide an equal-token single-agent deliberation control, role or round ablations, repeated stochastic runs, decoding settings, confidence intervals, or significance tests.
headline_results: Averaged across dataset groups, vulnerability categories, and prompt variants, the paper reports multi-role relative increases of 13.48% in precision, 18.25% in recall, and 16.13% in F1 over the single-role approach.

The benefit is not independent of prevalence. The authors report more obvious recall and F1 improvement when vulnerable examples are more common; absolute multi-role F1 values are roughly 0.796-0.875 in the 80%-vulnerable group but only 0.344-0.380 in the 20%-vulnerable group.
An example attributes a corrected false positive to the developer pointing out that wcsncat and its size argument prevent the alleged buffer overflow, after which the tester changes its judgment.
The reported accuracy improvement requires a 484% increase in consumed tokens, and no latency or monetary-cost result is given.

This is a two-page preliminary classification study on code segments, not evidence of project-scale vulnerability discovery, confirmed defects, production deployment, or operational security improvement.
limitations: Only one model version, four vulnerability categories, and short C/C++ snippets are tested.
The large token-budget mismatch prevents attributing the result solely to distinct roles rather than added deliberation.
Results vary strongly with class balance, and low absolute precision/F1 in the mostly non-vulnerable group implies substantial false-positive review burden.
No repeated-run reliability, decoding parameters, inferential statistics, calibration, adversarial evaluation, or production study is reported.
The tester remains the final authority even when maximum depth is reached, and the paper does not measure unresolved disagreement or harmful persuasion between roles.
future_work: Integrate in-context learning examples to guide the agents toward better collaboration during discussion.
combinable_methods: Independent tester judgment before exposing it to a developer perspective.
Bounded developer-tester dialogue with a consensus or depth-based stopping condition.
Binary decisions paired with concise rationales so disagreements can target specific claims.
In-context collaboration examples combined with explicit token budgets and class-balanced evaluation.

evidence_notes.research_design: GPTLens separates open-ended smart-contract auditing into high-temperature candidate generation by one or two GPT-4 Auditor instances and low-temperature discrimination by a GPT-4 Critic that scores correctness, severity, and profitability. Thirteen Etherscan contracts with CVE-reported vulnerabilities are tested in six configurations: a one-output Auditor baseline; one Auditor producing up to three candidates followed by random, Critic, or oracle selection; and two Auditors producing up to three candidates each followed by Critic or oracle selection. Auditors use temperature 0.7, the Critic temperature 0, and every configuration is run for three trials. A trial counts only when function, vulnerability, and reasoning align with the CVE report.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: All non-oracle configurations use GPT-4, the same 13 contracts, the same CVE labels, and top-1 evaluation. The interventions are not budget matched: the baseline generates one candidate, while GPTLens generates up to three or six and adds a separate Critic call. Oracle variants use ground truth and are upper bounds, not deployable baselines. The paper reports no token, latency, monetary-cost, equal-call single-agent, repeated-seed, significance, or component-prompt control.
headline_results: With one Auditor producing up to three candidates plus a Critic, the contract-level hit ratio rises from 38.5% for one-stage one-candidate auditing to 76.9%, and the trial-level ratio rises from 33.3% to 46.2%.
Adding a second Auditor raises the Critic-selected trial hit ratio from 46.2% to 59.0%, but contract coverage falls from 76.9% to 69.2%; additional agents therefore do not improve every metric.

Randomly selecting among three candidates lowers trial accuracy to 18.0% from the one-candidate baseline's 33.3%, while increasing contract coverage from 38.5% to 46.2%. Diversity broadens recall but worsens top-1 precision without effective discrimination.
The two-Auditor oracle reaches 74.4% trial hits versus 59.0% for the Critic, leaving a substantial ranking gap; three of 13 contracts have zero successful trials in every reported configuration.

The study uses real exploited contracts, but only offline CVE-label matching. It does not measure deployment, prevented losses, analyst workload, novel-vulnerability confirmation, or replacement of manual audit.
limitations: Thirteen contracts and three trials per setting provide preliminary evidence without uncertainty estimates or significance tests.
The apparent multi-role gain is confounded with extra stochastic samples and Critic inference; there is no equal-token or equal-call single-agent control.
The Critic is the same model family that generated the candidates and is not grounded in execution, static analysis, formal verification, or human adjudication during selection.
Known CVE reports are incomplete labels for any other valid findings, so potentially real but unexploited vulnerabilities can be counted as false positives under the task definition.
Token limits prevent testing larger candidate pools, scoring across batches can be inconsistent even at low temperature, and no runtime or cost measurements are supplied.
future_work: Develop prompts and diversity metrics that increase auditing diversity without increasing the candidate count.
Use in-context examples to improve Critic score consistency across batches.
Adapt chain-of-thought, tree-of-thoughts, and cumulative reasoning to vulnerability detection.
Explore additional specialist roles and richer collaboration protocols.
Allow agents to invoke external knowledge, tools, or APIs and use LLMs as assistants to developers and auditors rather than only as an end-to-end detector.
combinable_methods: High-temperature independent candidate generation followed by low-temperature ranking.
Structured JSON handoffs containing the function, vulnerability, and rationale.
Multi-criteria Critic scoring for correctness, severity, and attacker profitability.
External static, dynamic, symbolic, or formal evidence to ground Critic decisions.
Human auditor review for top-ranked findings, with false positives and analyst effort measured explicitly.

evidence_notes.research_design: INTERVENOR uses a Code Learner to generate or repair code and a Code Teacher to turn compiler or test failures into a natural-language Chain-of-Repair before the Learner tries again. Main agents use gpt-3.5-turbo-0613 at temperature 0.2, maximum length 512, zero-shot prompts, and at most five repair turns; additional pairings use CodeLlama-7B/13B. Evaluation covers HumanEval, MBPP, multilingual HumanEval-X, DS-1000, and the 4,463-example CodeError repair set. Studies compare published model baselines, no repair, direct error-message repair, Self-Refine, one- versus multi-turn CoR, Teacher/Learner model pairings, error types, and API calls per repair turn.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: The most informative prompt study builds all conditions on GPT-3.5 and uses the same task datasets; Table 10 reports two calls per INTERVENOR and Self-Refine turn, providing a close call-count control for planned repair versus self-reflection. However, the headline no-repair GPT-3.5 baseline receives fewer calls, most Table 2 baseline results are borrowed from other papers, and prompts and feedback differ by design. Tokens, latency, monetary cost, execution hardware, repeated runs, and an equal-transcript monolithic controller are not controlled.
headline_results: INTERVENOR reaches 75.6% and 69.8% pass@1 on HumanEval and MBPP versus 60.3% and 39.8% for unassisted GPT-3.5. Across the reported code-generation and translation tasks, the authors summarize gains over GPT-3.5 as about 18% and 4.3%, respectively.

In the all-GPT-3.5 prompt study, one-turn CoR averages 53.6 across five generation tasks plus CodeError, versus 51.4 for direct compiler messages and 50.2 for Self-Refine; multi-turn CoR averages 61.6. After three turns on the five generation datasets, CoR averages 66.7 versus 63.0 for Self-Refine and 62.9 for direct error messages.

Teacher capability matters. With a fixed GPT-3.5 Learner on HumanEval, no intervention scores 60.3, a CodeLlama-7B Teacher 65.2, CodeLlama-13B 66.5, and GPT-3.5 Teacher 69.5. The same ordering appears broadly across datasets.

On CodeError, one-turn CoR scores 15.9 versus 9.8 for direct error messages and 5.2 for Self-Refine; multi-turn CoR reaches 21.7. The paper attributes the gain to compiler-grounded diagnosis of assertion, name, syntax, type, and other errors.
Table 10 gives INTERVENOR and Self-Refine the same two calls per repair turn, while Self-Debug uses three and Self-Collaboration more than three; it reports no token, latency, or dollar comparison.
The work evaluates benchmark programs and collected buggy submissions, not repository maintenance or production operation, and it does not assess generated-code security or safe execution.
limitations: Effectiveness depends on the foundation model's ability to diagnose errors and follow repair instructions; weak Teachers and Learners reduce gains.
Compilers expose syntax/runtime errors, but logical-error repair depends on the availability, robustness, and coverage of tests.
The strongest absolute comparison gives INTERVENOR multiple repair calls while the no-repair baseline gets one generation; only Self-Refine is closely matched by calls per turn.
Temperature is fixed at 0.2, but no repeated-run variance, confidence intervals, or statistical tests are reported, and many headline baselines are imported.
No repository-scale task, production deployment, security analysis, sandbox model, token accounting, latency, monetary cost, or energy result is provided.
future_work: Extend the mechanism to feedback from other environments or rule systems, which the authors identify as a route for evolving LLM behavior.
Address the two explicit dependencies identified in the limitations: stronger foundation-model diagnosis and more robust, comprehensive test feedback.
combinable_methods: Compiler and test execution followed by a specialist diagnosis-and-plan stage before code repair.
A stronger Teacher paired with a cheaper Learner when model-routing cost is measured.
Bounded iterative repair with early termination when all tests pass.
Detailed error type, location, failing input, and expected output as structured repair context.
Broader tests or rule-system feedback to expose logical failures that compilers cannot detect.

evidence_notes.research_design: The paper uses a four-phase review workflow: exploratory review of software-engineering LLM multi-agent systems, targeted review of metric studies and documentation, citation snowballing from a prior literature review with selection based on relevance, reproducibility, and methodological clarity, and catalogue construction. Systems must generate or execute code, use multi-agent collaboration, and define applicable software-development metrics. The authors consolidate 26 existing and 12 proposed metrics into Outcome, Process, Product, and Framework categories, preserving original definitions where possible.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: This is a metric catalogue, not an empirical comparison, and it deliberately excludes single-agent systems; it therefore cannot establish a specialist multi-agent advantage. The reviewed frameworks use heterogeneous datasets, objectives, and self-defined measures. The paper provides inclusion criteria but no reproducible search strings, corpus counts, quality appraisal, inter-rater procedure, or validation of the 12 proposed metrics. Controlled cross-framework comparison is explicitly future work.
headline_results: The catalogue contains 38 metrics: outcome measures such as requirements met and pass@k; process measures such as duration, tokens, utterances, iterations, rework, and per-agent use; product measures such as errors, dead code, and messages per line; and framework measures for human involvement and ease of use.

The review finds equivalent concepts under different names and identically named metrics measuring different constructs, which can make isolated frameworks appear optimal and prevent direct comparison.

The 12 proposed metrics add K-executions to success, ease of use, Sounds Good, rework ratio, human clarification count/score, iteration count, time per iteration, tokens per agent, messages/LOC, dead code, and framework ease of use.

Traditional code-quality measures such as complexity, duplication, code smells, and test coverage were not identified in the reviewed framework evaluations; the authors recommend adding them as complementary Product measures.

The complete catalogue has no explicit metric for vulnerability rate, safety/security violations, fault tolerance, recovery, or stochastic run variance. Its listed cost metric operationalizes cost as total tokens, so production cost and reliability require additional measures.
The contribution is a maintained evaluation artifact and research agenda, not evidence that any architecture is production ready or better than a matched single agent.
limitations: Single-agent systems are excluded by design, so the catalogue cannot support a controlled single-versus-multi conclusion.
The 12 new metrics have not yet been systematically validated for relevance, construct validity, or cross-context applicability.
Framework discovery and metric reconstruction are insufficiently specified for full review reproducibility, and some measures were inferred from logs, appendices, or result tables.
Preserving original metric definitions exposes fragmentation but does not normalize units, formulas, datasets, budgets, or model/tool conditions.
Security, fault tolerance, nondeterministic stability, monetary cost, and operational incident measures remain absent from the catalogue.
future_work: Systematically validate every identified metric across contexts.
Run controlled cross-framework comparisons using the catalogue.
Expand analysis to less-studied frameworks and refine the metrics into a standardized, reproducible, conceptually grounded methodology.
Maintain the open-source catalogue through versioning and community contributions.
combinable_methods: Evaluate Outcome, Process, Product, and Framework dimensions together rather than reporting task success alone.
Pair requirement fulfillment and executable tests with iterations, rework, time, calls, input/output tokens, and per-agent resource use.
Add human clarification frequency, clarification quality, human involvement, and usability to deployment evaluations.
Combine the catalogue with complexity, duplication, code-smell, test-coverage, security, fault-injection, and repeated-run stability measures.
Use one versioned metric specification across matched models, prompts, tools, datasets, and budgets in future cross-framework experiments.

quotes.text: Frameworks often rely on self-defined or inconsistent metrics, hindering reproducibility and making frameworks appear optimal within their own settings, which obscures the true state of the art and can produce artificially inflated performance results.
quotes.use: Explains why unmatched framework claims cannot answer the focal comparison reliably.

quotes.text: We propose 12 novel metrics, combine them with 26 existing ones, resulting in a structured catalogue of 38 metrics across four technical categories: Outcome, Process, Product, and Framework.
quotes.use: States the catalogue's scope and organizing dimensions.

quotes.text: These proposed metrics aim to reduce fragmentation and provide a foundation for more rigorous, reproducible, and comparable assessments.
quotes.use: States the intended method for improving evaluation rigor.

quotes.text: It is worth noting that traditional software engineering metrics were not identified among the assessment practices of the analysed frameworks.
quotes.use: Documents a product-quality measurement gap.

quotes.text: Building on this catalogue, we aim to perform controlled cross-framework comparisons and explore less-studied frameworks, refining our proposed metrics toward a standardised, reproducible, and conceptually grounded evaluation methodology for LLM-based multi-agent systems in software development.
quotes.use: Shows that controlled comparative validation remains future work.
